title: Senior At-Home Care
desc: Plan and deliver safe, respectful at-home support for older adults: daily living, safety, medicines reminders, dignity and when to call for help.
outcomes: Explain the needs, rights and dignity of an older person at home.
Find fall, fire and medicine risks in a home.
Judge when a situation needs a professional or emergency help.
Build a written care routine and a family communication plan.
task: Produce a person-centred home care plan for a practice case, with a home safety check, daily routine, emergency card and carer wellbeing plan.
condition: A practice case or a consenting family, a phone, forms, two peers and a qualified nurse or care mentor. Nursing procedures are outside scope.
standard: Plan respects the person's wishes; safety check finds and fixes at least 8 risks; emergency card is complete; no clinical task is done outside training; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Family carers, home-care assistants, community volunteers, care entrepreneurs.
evidence: care plan, home safety checklist, routine, emergency card, carer plan
modules: Respect and dignity first
Understand
Good care starts with the person, not the task. Older adults have a lifetime of skills, habits and choices that care must protect.
Ask how the person likes to be addressed and what matters to them.
Offer choices; do not decide for them when they can decide.
Protect privacy in washing, dressing and toilet care.
Speak slowly and clearly, face to face, without talking over them.
Mrs A prefers tea before washing. The carer keeps this order and tells her each step. Her morning takes ten minutes longer and she is calmer and more willing to help.
Write a one-page "about me" profile for a practice case.
Profile has routines, likes, fears and decisions the person makes alone.
Home safety check
Analyse
Most harm to older people at home is preventable. A structured check finds risks before an accident.
Falls: rugs, loose cables, wet floors, poor light, steps without rails.
Bathroom: non-slip mat, grab rails, raised seat.
Fire and gas: working smoke alarm, safe cooking habits, switch-off reminders.
Access: keys for helpers, clear path for emergency crews, phone within reach.
A check finds a loose rug, a dark stair and no bathroom rail. The rug is removed, a night light is fitted and a rail is ordered, with dates and who is responsible.
Complete a room-by-room safety checklist and a fix list.
Every room is checked, each risk has a fix, a date and an owner.
Daily living support
Apply
Support independence rather than replacing it.
Break tasks into steps and help with the step that is hard.
Offer enough time; rushing causes accidents and loss of confidence.
Use aids: long-handled tools, easy-grip cutlery, pill boxes.
Watch eating, drinking, skin and sleep and record changes.
Mr B used to skip lunch. A simple routine of a set time, a favourite dish and a drink by the chair raises his daily intake and he regains weight in a month.
Design a daily routine for a practice case.
Routine covers meals, drinks, washing, movement, rest and social time with timings.
Medicines and health reminders
Apply
Carers remind and observe; clinicians decide.
Use a weekly pill box and a written list from the doctor or pharmacist.
Never change doses or stop medicines on your own.
Note side effects such as dizziness, confusion or rash and report them.
Keep medicines locked away from others in the house.
The carer notices a new sleepiness after a medicine change, records the time and calls the clinic, which adjusts the dose.
Create a medicine reminder chart and a reporting note.
Chart shows names, times and checks; note shows what, when and who was told.
Mind, mood and memory
Apply
Loneliness, low mood and forgetfulness are common but not inevitable.
Keep routine, light, daily walks and social contact.
Use calendars, clear labels and a daily board for memory.
Respond calmly to repeated questions; do not argue.
Seek advice if mood or memory changes quickly.
A weekly phone call from a grandchild and a neighbour tea visit reduce low mood; a clock with the day and date reduces repeated questions.
Plan a week of social and mental activity.
Plan has at least five activities, one with another person each day.
Emergencies and when to call
Evaluate
Know the line between watching and acting.
Call at once for chest pain, trouble breathing, stroke signs, serious bleeding or a head injury.
Call the clinic the same day for fever, new confusion or a bad fall without injury.
Keep numbers, medical history and medicine list on a card by the phone.
Practise the plan with the family.
After a fall with no visible injury, the carer notes new confusion, which is a warning sign, and calls for help instead of waiting.
Write the one-page emergency card.
Card has numbers, conditions, medicines, allergies and clear call-now signs.
Family and carer wellbeing
Evaluate
Carers burn out when they carry everything alone.
Share tasks and agree a rota.
Take breaks, sleep and eat properly; ask for respite.
Join a carer group or call a helpline.
Watch for stress signs such as anger, tiredness and withdrawal.
A daughter who was caring alone adds two relatives to a rota. She gets two free evenings a week and her stress falls.
Make a carer wellbeing plan with a weekly rota.
Plan has shared tasks, breaks and a named support contact.
Review and improve
Create
Care plans change as needs change.
Review monthly or after any health change.
Ask the person and the family what is working.
Record incidents and learn from them.
Update the plan and tell everyone involved.
After two near-falls the review adds a walking aid and physiotherapy advice, and the next month shows no falls.
Produce the full care plan pack with a review date.
All sections are present, personal details are respected, and the next review is scheduled.
quiz: Why use their words?
It keeps dignity and choice. (Covered in module 1: Respect and dignity first. To pass that module: Profile has routines, likes, fears and decisions the person makes alone.)
Name three fall risks.
Loose rugs, poor light, wet floors. (Covered in module 2: Home safety check. To pass that module: Every room is checked, each risk has a fix, a date and an owner.)
Who decides doses?
The prescriber. (Covered in module 3: Daily living support. To pass that module: Routine covers meals, drinks, washing, movement, rest and social time with timings.)
When call emergency?

Chest pain, stroke signs, serious fall, breathing trouble. (Covered in module 4: Medicines and health reminders. To pass that module: Chart shows names, times and checks; note shows what, when and who was told.)
What is "do with, not for"?
Support independence by helping only as needed. (Covered in module 5: Mind, mood and memory. To pass that module: Plan has at least five activities, one with another person each day.)
Name one mood tip.
Daily activity and social contact. (Covered in module 6: Emergencies and when to call. To pass that module: Card has numbers, conditions, medicines, allergies and clear call-now signs.)
What is sudden confusion a sign of?
Possible illness; seek help. (Covered in module 7: Family and carer wellbeing. To pass that module: Plan has shared tasks, breaks and a named support contact.)
What goes on an emergency card?
Numbers, allergies, medicines, contacts. (Covered in module 8: Review and improve. To pass that module: All sections are present, personal details are respected, and the next review is scheduled.)
Why carer breaks?
To avoid burnout. (Covered in module 8: Review and improve. To pass that module: All sections are present, personal details are respected, and the next review is scheduled.)
How often review?
Monthly or after any event. (Covered in module 8: Review and improve. To pass that module: All sections are present, personal details are respected, and the next review is scheduled.)
rubric: Every claim linked to a dated record and checked by a peer
